rv.q: This is bracingly good and important.
It is a truly awesome spectacle, and a monumental shift in tone from Frecknall, whose work has always previously felt intimate and warm - always underpinned by a sense of her characters’ decency.
Hattie Morahan as Helene and Stuart Thompson as Osvald bring a mesmerising intensity to this mother-son dance of death, and there’s welcome black comedy from Paul Hilton as the self-serving priest.
This isn’t Frecknall’s finest moment – it’s hard to avoid melodrama with Lorca, and this production does often feel overwrought.
This is not a play that ends well for anyone.
Everything is intelligent, but the purpose is too evident.
Ultimately, the stylised elements smother the play’s intensity.
It takes too long to ignite, yet this slow-burn staging flickers with a kind of compulsion.
There are powerful moments, but so much of this story’s passion seeps away, lost on stony ground.
But by the end, you long to escape from this overwrought battle of wills and step out into the sunshine.
For all its tragic ending, it's a plod of an evening, surprisingly cool (it's meant to be baking hot) and with an added layer of trowelled-on feminism.
It’s a superb night of theatre, a new look at a difficult but always timely play.
It’s terrifically conceived and staged, Alice Birch’s excellent adaptation adds new layers to the play’s complexity.
However, not all audiences will appreciate this hand on the back of their necks.
Federico Garcia Lorca’s play is one of the greatest of the 20th century, but its power is consistently undermined by the staging.
What a muddle this show is. All the tragic elements are ludicrous and all the farcical elements are tedious.
It’s a powerful and thought-provoking play which unfolds on one of the most impressive-looking sets we’ve seen, and the acting performances are universally strong.
This modern-feeling version highlights the psychological plight of the women trapped in the eponymous house.
Just about everything in this production is wrong.

cn.t: Frecknall's visually striking production, featuring a standout ensemble led by Harriet Walter, divides critics with its bold staging and Birch's modern adaptation—some find it desolately powerful, others overly clinical and heavy-handed.
